summary: A Complaint Feedback Loop lets mailbox providers tell senders when users report their mail as spam. This experimental document defines a header field in which a message originator names its feedback address, plus rules for processing and forwarding complaints. It aims to replace a manual, time-consuming setup with an automated one.

plainLanguage.summary: A letter can carry a line saying "if you didn't like this, tell me here." That way complaints reach the sender without lots of phone calls.

questions: how to receive spam complaints automatically
subtitle: Automated feedback loop for email spam complaints without manual setup.

tldr.problem: Mailbox providers must tell senders when users mark their email as spam, but setting up complaint feedback loops requires manual work from both the sender and the provider, which does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: A message originator adds a CFBL-Address header field naming where spam complaints should go, cryptographically signed with DKIM to verify ownership. Mailbox providers read this header and send complaints there automatically.
tldr.outcome: Senders get automated feedback without manual per-provider registration. Mailbox providers can support feedback loops with less operational burden. This is an experimental protocol to test whether the approach works in practice.

today: RFC 9477 is an Experimental protocol and has not been obsoleted. It is a living experiment to test whether automated feedback loops reduce operational burden for senders and mailbox providers.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Email providers have a responsibility to tell senders when recipients mark their mail as spam. This is called a complaint feedback loop. Today, senders must register with each mailbox provider individually: filling out forms, verifying they own the domain, arranging for the provider to accept reports. The process is manual and slow, and smaller mailbox providers often skip it entirely because the overhead is too high.

This RFC proposes a simpler way: senders add two new header fields to their email messages. The CFBL-Address header names the email address where the sender wants to receive complaints. The CFBL-Feedback-ID header optionally holds an identifier the sender can use to track which message the complaint refers to. Both headers are signed using DKIM, the same mechanism that authenticates email domains. When a mailbox provider sees these headers, it can automatically forward spam complaints to the address named, without any out-of-band setup.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of calling on the phone to tell someone you don't want their mail, you send a note to the address they wrote on the envelope. The envelope is sealed with their signature to prove they own it.

sections.title: Rules for Safety and Ownership
sections.content:
The mechanism includes strict rules to prevent forgery and abuse. If the message's From domain and the CFBL-Address domain are the same, the domain must be signed with a valid DKIM signature. If the CFBL-Address is a subdomain of the From domain, the From domain's DKIM signature is enough. If the CFBL-Address is at a completely different domain, both domains must be signed, proving that both own the address.

The feedback message itself must be an ARF (Abuse Reporting Format) report or XARF (eXtended ARF), and it must be signed by the mailbox provider's domain. The sender's side can optionally include a CFBL-Feedback-ID with an HMAC-based token instead of plaintext, making it harder for attackers to guess and forge complaints. To protect user privacy, the mailbox provider can omit or redact the email body and headers, sending only the required fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides sign their work to prove it is real. The sender's signature proves the address is theirs. The mailbox provider's signature proves the complaint came from them. Both can be checked to spot forgery.

sections.title: Header Field Syntax
sections.content:
The CFBL-Address header field holds an email address and an optional report type. For example: CFBL-Address: fbl@example.com; report=arf. The address MUST be RFC 5322 compliant. The report type is either arf for Abuse Reporting Format or xarf for extended format. If omitted, ARF is the default.

The CFBL-Feedback-ID header is a free-form identifier the sender creates. It can hold plaintext, but the RFC recommends using an HMAC with a secret key so that attackers cannot guess IDs. Both headers must be included in the DKIM signature's h= tag to protect them from modification in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: The From address is like the envelope's return address. The CFBL-Address is where the mailbox provider sends the complaint form. Both need the sender's signature to be trusted.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
The CFBL address can be flooded with mail like any email address, but this is not a new problem. An automatic account suspension on the first complaint could block legitimate senders (for example, a sender sharing photos with friends could be marked as spam by one person). Senders must use caution before suspending accounts.

An attacker could send forged ARF reports to guess identifiers and cause false unsubscribes. The CFBL-Feedback-ID field prevents this if senders use an HMAC. Another risk: the mailbox provider could leak that an address exists by generating a complaint when the user manually reports spam, which the sender then sees as proof of the address. Providers should use reputation data to avoid this.

The RFC allows providers to omit or redact personal data from feedback messages to comply with data privacy laws like GDPR and CCPA. Messages can be sent with only the Message-ID and CFBL-Feedback-ID, with all personal information removed.
sections.plainLanguage: The system trusts both sides to sign their work. If someone lies about a signature, it gets caught. People have to be careful not to block accounts too fast on complaints, and providers should not send too many complaints to annoying senders.

sections.title: Working Examples
sections.content:
A simple example: a newsletter includes CFBL-Address: fbl@example.com; report=arf and CFBL-Feedback-ID: 111:222:333:4444 headers. The message is signed with the sender's DKIM key. When a user marks it as spam, the mailbox provider creates an ARF report and sends it to fbl@example.com.

A privacy-safe example: the provider can send only the CFBL-Feedback-ID without the message body or other sensitive headers. An advanced example uses an HMAC-based CFBL-Feedback-ID like 3789e1ae1938aa2f0dfdfa48b20d8f8bc6c21ac34fc5023d63f9e64a43dfedc0 (a 64-character hex string). This makes it nearly impossible for attackers to forge complaints by guessing the identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender puts the headers in every email they send. When a recipient says "I do not want this," the mailbox provider follows the headers to send a report to the address the sender named.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 9477 is an Experimental protocol published in September 2023. It was published through the Independent RFC Stream, not the IETF standards process. The goal is to gather feedback from implementers and mailbox providers on whether this approach is practical and whether it reduces operational burden. Success is defined as adoption by at least one major mailbox provider and two message originators within two years, using the headers to exchange real feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an experimental idea being tested to see if it works in the real world. People are trying it out to see if it is better than the old way.
